---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/hoppscotch/hoppscotch
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: hoppscotch/hoppscotch:2026.7.0
  port: 80
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2", with db_extensions pg_trgm)
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: hoppscotch
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ THE DECISION TO PUT TO THE USER BEFORE ANYTHING IS CREATED: YOU NEED AN AUTH PROVIDER READY, OR THE INSTANCE CANNOT BE CLAIMED AND WILL SIT OPEN. Hoppscotch cannot be signed into until an auth provider is configured, and helper.ts:15 shows the complete list of settings an environment variable can seed into the config table: PROXY_APP_URL, and nothing else. So the provider is configured through the onboarding wizard AFTER the URL is live, not in the compose. Before you deploy, have ONE of these in hand: SMTP credentials for magic-link e-mail (an SMTP URL and a from address), or a Google, GitHub or Microsoft OAuth app. For the OAuth route the redirect URI is derived, not chosen: helper.ts:587-627 builds it as <VITE_BACKEND_API_URL>/auth/<provider>/callback, which in this recipe is https://<your-dname>/backend/v1/auth/<provider>/callback. Generate the dname yourself up front so the OAuth app can be registered before the deploy."
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: THE FIRST PERSON TO SIGN IN, AND NOTHING ELSE CLOSES THE WINDOW. auth.service.ts:371-386 (verifyAdmin) elevates the signed-in user to admin whenever the total user count is exactly 1. Worse, the setup that comes before it is anonymous: onboarding.controller.ts declares POST /v1/onboarding/config with only a rate-limit guard and NO authentication, and infra-config.service.ts:538-546 keeps it re-runnable for as long as usersCount is 0. So between the container going healthy and you signing in, any stranger who finds the hostname can point the instance's authentication at their own SMTP server or their own OAuth app, sign in, and become its administrator. There is no env var, no default account and no setting that prevents this. COMPLETE THE ONBOARDING AND SIGN IN YOURSELF AS PART OF THE DEPLOY, BEFORE YOU HAND OVER THE URL, then run the status check in this file to prove the seat is taken."
  - "IS REGISTRATION OPEN AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT? YES, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF THE ADMIN DASHBOARD. Any further person who can satisfy the configured provider (any e-mail address if you chose magic links, any account on the OAuth app if you chose SSO) can create an account; they simply are not admins, because verifyAdmin only elevates when the user count is exactly 1. Restrict it where the provider is defined: a Google or GitHub OAuth app you control, or an SMTP setup plus the admin dashboard's user management. Say to the user which of those they are relying on."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS VISITOR CAN REACH, STATED PLAINLY: the Hoppscotch app itself, by design. It is a browser-side API client and it works without an account, keeping that person's collections in their own browser. Requests they fire go from their browser, or through PROXY_APP_URL, which defaults to Hoppscotch's own hosted proxy and NOT to your VM (helper.ts:349-352), so this is not free compute or a request relay on your machine. What they must not reach unclaimed is the onboarding endpoint above. There is no configuration flag in InfraConfigEnum that puts the app itself behind a login; if the user needs that, this is the wrong tool and a private network is the answer."
  - "⛔ SET DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY TO EXACTLY 32 CHARACTERS AND REUSE THE SAME VALUE ON EVERY REDEPLOY. src/utils.ts:336,344-356 keys aes-256-cbc with Buffer.from(DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY), so anything other than 32 bytes throws on the first encrypt. It protects the rows in the infra_config table, which include the auto-generated JWT_SECRET and SESSION_SECRET and the SMTP and OAuth secrets you enter in the wizard. ✅ THIS ONE FAILS LOUDLY RATHER THAN SILENTLY, WHICH IS UNUSUAL FOR THIS LIBRARY: helper.ts:100-112 catches ERR_OSSL_BAD_DECRYPT and raises ENV_INVALID_DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY, so a redeploy with a different key refuses to start rather than quietly resetting your configuration. Generate it with 'openssl rand -hex 16', which is 32 characters, and store it with the deployment."
  - "⛔ THE IMAGE DOES NOT RUN ITS OWN MIGRATIONS. aio_run.mjs starts Caddy, the backend and the webapp server, and nothing else; the repo's own compose has a SEPARATE hoppscotch-migrate service for this. The one place upstream shows the command against the image is docker-compose.deploy.yml:40-46, 'pnpm exec prisma migrate deploy && node /usr/src/app/aio_run.mjs' (that file's first line calls itself internal and not for personal deployments, so take the command from it, not the stack). Override the service command in your compose with exactly that, run through sh -c. The image's WORKDIR is already /dist/backend, where the prisma schema and CLI live. Skip it and the backend starts against an empty database and fails on its first query."
  - "⛔ PASS db_extensions WITH pg_trgm WHEN YOU PROVISION THE DATABASE. prisma/migrations/20240226053141_full_text_search_additions/migration.sql:4-5 runs CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm. pg_trgm is on redu's own extension allowlist, so redu creates it as the superuser at provision time and the migration's IF NOT EXISTS becomes a no-op. Without it you are betting on the managed role being allowed to create the extension itself, and if that bet loses the migration aborts partway and the app comes up against a half-built schema. If you somehow hit a permission-denied-to-create-extension error anyway, re-provision with db_superuser true rather than guessing at grants."
  - "ONE DATABASE ONLY, WHICH KEEPS THIS ENTRY CLEAR OF THE TRAP THAT BROKE TWO OTHERS. redu's managed Postgres serves exactly one database and refuses any other at authentication with SQLSTATE 28000, superuser or not. Hoppscotch declares a single Prisma datasource reading DATABASE_URL and applies migrations in place; it never creates a second database. So database:'managed' with the default role, plus the pg_trgm extension above, and no db_superuser."
  - "⛔ RUN IT IN SUBPATH MODE OR IT NEEDS FOUR PORTS. Set ENABLE_SUBPATH_BASED_ACCESS=true and publish container port 80. aio-subpath-access.Caddyfile then puts everything behind one Caddy: the app at /, the admin dashboard at /admin, the backend reverse-proxied at /backend*, and the desktop bundle server at /desktop-app-server*. The DEFAULT is multiport mode, which binds 3000, 3100, 3170 and 3200 and cannot be exposed through a single redu hostname. Health probe: GET /backend/ping, which returns the body Success (app.controller.ts:4-10). ⚠️ HOPP_ALTERNATE_PORT only has an effect in subpath mode; in multiport mode aio_run.mjs prints a warning and ignores it."
  - "⛔ SET EVERY VITE_* URL TO THE REAL PUBLIC HOSTNAME AT DEPLOY TIME, NOT AFTERWARDS. aio_run.mjs:97-116 collects every VITE_* variable from the container environment and rewrites them into the already-built frontend bundle with import-meta-env, at container start. That means they are read once per start, they must be right before the first start, and changing one later needs a container restart to take effect. Generate the dname yourself in full <app>-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form first, then set: VITE_BASE_URL and VITE_SHORTCODE_BASE_URL to https://<dname>, VITE_ADMIN_URL to https://<dname>/admin, VITE_BACKEND_GQL_URL to https://<dname>/backend/graphql, VITE_BACKEND_WS_URL to wss://<dname>/backend/graphql, and VITE_BACKEND_API_URL to https://<dname>/backend/v1. Get VITE_BASE_URL wrong and you also lose secure cookies: helper.ts:579-581 sets ALLOW_SECURE_COOKIES purely from whether that URL starts with https."
  - "⛔ WHITELISTED_ORIGINS IS NOT OPTIONAL AND ITS ABSENCE IS A CRASH, NOT A WARNING. src/main.ts:57-62: in production the app calls configService.get('WHITELISTED_ORIGINS').split(','), and the aio image sets PRODUCTION=true at prod.Dockerfile:288, so an unset value is a TypeError during boot. Set it to https://<dname>. The upstream .env.example ships a list of localhost ports plus app://hoppscotch; keep app://hoppscotch only if the user actually intends to use the desktop app against this instance."
  - "SET TRUST_PROXY=true. It defaults to false (.env.example) and src/main.ts:81-84 only calls express's trust proxy when it is the string 'true'. Behind redu's TLS edge every request otherwise appears to come from the proxy's address, which collapses the per-IP rate limiter into a single global bucket. That matters more here than in most entries, because the rate limiter is the ONLY guard in front of the unauthenticated onboarding endpoint."
  - "NOTHING NEEDS A VOLUME, WHICH IS RARE. All durable state (users, collections, teams, and the encrypted infra_config rows) lives in the managed Postgres. The container writes only ephemeral things: /tmp for the import-meta-env rewrite and Caddy's storage (XDG_DATA_HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME are both set to /tmp at prod.Dockerfile:314-315), and /data/webapp-server for the webapp server's signing key, which is regenerated if lost. Mount a volume on /data/webapp-server only if the user cares about that key surviving a redeploy."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO FIGURE. Neither compose file in the repo sets a deploy.resources block and the README states no requirement, so there is no number to quote. What runs in the one container is a Caddy, a NestJS backend and a small Go static server, all from a pulled image with no build step, which is why m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB) is the starting point rather than something larger. Measure idle memory on the first real run and write the number back into this file rather than repeating this paragraph."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> confirm with the user which auth provider they will use and that its credentials or OAuth app are ready -> generate the dname -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr, roughly GBP 33 a month, inside the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small; OMITTING db_flavor_id defaults the database VM to the app flavor and roughly doubles the bill), db_extensions containing pg_trgm, port 80. ⚠️ plan_deploy upsizes a compose stack to m1.large once needs_compose is declared; pass flavor_id explicitly, because that larger floor exists for apps that BUILD from source and this image is pulled. Then complete the onboarding and sign in BEFORE handing over the URL."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built. Write the one-service docker-compose.yml locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. ⛔ Do NOT copy either compose file out of the repository: both build from source with a build: key, docker-compose.yml also starts its own bundled postgres:15 with a hardcoded credential, and docker-compose.deploy.yml opens by saying in capitals that it is not to be used for personal deployments."
  - "LICENCE: plain MIT, verified from LICENSE:1-21, with no addendum and no network clause. Nothing to reason about for a self-hoster; the only obligation is retaining the notice. Note that some features are marked enterprise edition in the README's footnotes and are not part of what this deploys."
  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but keeps the managed Postgres, which holds every user, team and shared collection, and that database keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. Say that plainly before deleting, and use delete_database when the user really wants it gone. ⚠️ delete_database has timed out at the MCP layer twice while succeeding server-side; confirm with list_databases rather than retrying."

# Self-host Hoppscotch on redu

An API request builder your team shares, on infrastructure you own: one all-in-one container, a
managed Postgres beside it, and a public HTTPS URL that serves the app, the admin dashboard and the

SOURCE IS EITHER GIT OR UPLOAD, NEVER BOTH. For code that is not pushed, or is private, or needs fixing first: write the files locally, call prepare_upload, run the tar+curl block it returns, then pass the source_token and NO repo. ⚠️ prepare_upload EXCLUDES .env from the tarball by design, so secrets have to reach the VM another way (pass them to the deploy call, not in the tree).

A MANAGED DATABASE IS A SECOND VM WITH ITS OWN HOURLY RATE, and delete_deployment deliberately LEAVES IT BEHIND so your data survives the app. That means a teardown that stops at delete_deployment keeps billing a database nobody can reach. Call delete_database too, and say so to the user before either.

A MANAGED POSTGRES SERVES EXACTLY ONE DATABASE. pg_hba is evaluated before role privileges, so being superuser does not help. An app that wants a second database needs a second managed server. This has broken deploys that otherwise looked healthy.

get_deployment RETURNS THE MERGED redu.md ONLY WHEN IT FITS ITS RESPONSE BUDGET. Over budget - which is normal for a mature recipe or any large app - it withholds redu_md_markdown and returns redu_md_last_deploy_block plus redu_md_deploy_log_line instead. That is NOT an error and must not be retried: apply those two edits to the file on disk and change nothing else.

⛔ THE MERGE NEVER WRITES A NEW QUIRK. Whatever redu returns, it refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and nothing else. Every gotcha YOUR run discovered has to be typed into the quirks list by hand before you commit, or it is lost - and that list is the only part of the file that makes the next deploy cheaper.

Measured 8 times out of 8: declaring needs_compose makes it quote m1.large, roughly double the real requirement, because it cannot see that the images are pulled rather than built. THE MANAGED DATABASE PASSWORD IS ON THE VM, NOT IN THE API. list_databases returns private_ip, port, db_name and db_user and DELIBERATELY NOT the password, so an agent that looks for it there finds nothing and starts guessing. The deploy writes the whole connection set into the compose project's .env on the app VM. Call get_env_keys for the NAMES first (no SSH, values never leave the VM); only if you need an actual VALUE, SSH in (get_ssh_command) and read that one key, `sudo grep '^PGPASSWORD=' /opt/app-src/.env`. ⚠️ That file is chmod 600 root:root so it needs sudo, and the database is on the PRIVATE network - reachable from the app VM, never from a laptop.

YOU CAN READ A DEPLOY VM WITHOUT SSHING INTO IT, and four tools do it: get_containers (what is running, health, restarts, crashed ones included), get_container_logs (what the app actually printed - the tool for 'deployed fine but does not work'), get_resource_usage (memory, disk, load, OOM kills) and get_env_keys (which variables got wired, by name). ⛔ get_instance_logs is the SERIAL CONSOLE and is not your app's logs; build_log stops when the build does. SSH is still yours for everything else - a shell on a real machine is the point, not a fallback. ⭐ MEASURED over 38 deploys: of 241 ssh escapes, 146 (61%) were exactly these four things, and the four tools were called 11 times. They are faster than a login, they cost the VM nothing extra (the reading is already cached), and reaching for ssh to run `docker ps` is the single most common wasted minute in a deploy.

⛔ THE PRIMARY SURFACE'S HOSTNAME COMES FROM THE TOP-LEVEL dname, NOT FROM expose[0].dname, WHICH IS SILENTLY DISCARDED. Extra expose entries DO keep the dname you give them, so the two behave differently and nothing tells you. If an app bakes its own public URL into config at boot (CPAD_MAIN_DOMAIN, allowed_origins, SITE_URL), generate the full `<label>-<8 lowercase letters/digits>.redu.cloud` form yourself and pass it as the TOP-LEVEL dname, which is used verbatim. Passing it on expose[0] instead gets you an app configured for a hostname redu never created, answering 200 on a name it does not believe is its own.

WEBSOCKETS WORK THROUGH THE PROXY WITH NO CONFIGURATION: every proxy host redu creates has upgrade enabled. Measured at the protocol level, HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols with the subprotocol echoed back. ⚠️ TEST IT WITH `curl --http1.1`: plain curl negotiates HTTP/2, which has no Upgrade mechanism at all, so the app answers as an ordinary GET and the failure looks exactly like a proxy refusing to upgrade. Browsers use HTTP/1.1 for websockets regardless. Do not disable an app's realtime features on the strength of an HTTP/2 curl.
